# Why the sea rises and falls twice a day

The tide is the regular rise and fall of the sea surface along a coast. It is
easy to watch and surprisingly hard to explain, because the cause is not the
water being pulled toward the moon like a single lump. The cause is a
difference in pull.

## The cause: a difference in pull

The moon attracts every part of the Earth, but not equally. The side of the
planet facing the moon is closer, so it is pulled a little harder than the
centre of the planet, and the far side is pulled a little less. Physicists call
this uneven pull the tidal force. Because the solid Earth moves as one body and
the ocean is free to flow, the ocean responds to the differences: water on the
near side is drawn toward the moon relative to the planet, and water on the far
side is left behind relative to the planet. The result is two bulges of water,
one facing the moon and one facing away from it.

The Earth turns beneath these bulges once a day. A point on the coast therefore
passes through two high waters and two low waters in a little over a day. The
interval is slightly longer than twenty-four hours because the moon is itself
moving along its orbit, so the planet has to turn a bit further each day to
catch up with it. This is why high tide arrives roughly fifty minutes later
each day.

## The sun joins in

The sun also raises tides, but they are about half as strong as the lunar ones.
The sun is vastly more massive, yet it is so much farther away that the
difference in its pull across the Earth is small. What matters for tides is not
the strength of the pull but how quickly it changes with distance, and that
falls off steeply as the distance grows.

When the sun, Earth and moon lie roughly in a line, which happens at new moon
and full moon, the two sets of bulges add together. These large tides are
called spring tides, and the name has nothing to do with the season. When the
sun and moon pull at right angles to each other, at the quarter phases, the
solar bulges partly cancel the lunar ones. These small tides are called neap
tides. A full cycle from spring to neap and back takes about a fortnight.

## Why coasts differ so much

The open ocean rises only a fraction of a metre, yet some bays see changes of
more than ten metres. The local shape of the coast decides the outcome. A
funnel-shaped bay squeezes the incoming water into a narrowing space, which
raises its height. A basin can also have its own natural sloshing period, and
if that period is close to the tidal one, the water builds up in step with the
forcing, much as a child on a swing gains height from well-timed pushes. In
contrast, an almost enclosed sea such as the Mediterranean has very small tides
because little water can enter or leave through its narrow opening.

Some coasts have two high waters of similar height each day, which is called a
semidiurnal pattern. Others have only one high water a day, a diurnal pattern,
and many have a mixture in which the two highs differ clearly in height. Which
pattern a place shows depends on the tilt of the moon's orbit and on the shape
of the surrounding ocean basin.

## Common mix-ups

Tides are not the same as waves or currents, although a tidal current is the
horizontal flow of water that accompanies the vertical rise and fall. Wind and
air pressure also change sea level, and a storm surge can add a metre or more on
top of the predicted tide, which is why a forecast table gives the astronomical
tide only. Lakes have tides too, but they are tiny, because a small body of
water cannot develop a noticeable bulge.
